title: Mother Teresa
hookLine: a nun in a white sari kneels on a Calcutta pavement beside a dying stranger

cards: A man is lying on a pavement in Calcutta, the city now called Kolkata. People step around him. A small woman in a white cotton sari with blue edges stops, kneels, and touches his face.
She and another sister carry him to a long room near a temple, with low cots in rows. They wash him. They give him something to drink.
They ask his name. If he dies tonight, he'll die clean, with someone beside him who knows what he's called. The world came to know that woman as Mother Teresa.

teach.b: She was born Agnes, to an Albanian family in the Balkans, and became a nun with the Sisters of Loreto, teaching girls in a convent school in Calcutta.

Outside the school walls was another city: people sleeping, sick and dying in the streets. She later described a call within her call: to leave the convent and live among the poorest people she could find.
With her bishop's and the Church's permission, she did, and the community she started became the Missionaries of Charity. Underneath it all is a verse in Matthew.
Jesus describes the Son of man coming in glory to judge the nations, and the king tells people they fed him, clothed him, visited him. They're baffled: when?

teach.h: YE HAVE DONE IT UNTO ME.
teach.b: The answer, in the King James Bible: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." She took that literally.
She taught her sisters that the dying man on the pavement was Jesus, in what she called a distressing disguise. So the work wasn't, for her, social service with prayer added. It was the prayer.
Now the honest part: she has admirers and critics. Some doctors and journalists questioned the medical care in her homes and how donations were used.

And after her death, her private letters were published, showing that for long stretches she felt God was absent, a darkness she told almost no one about, while she kept getting up and going back to the cots.
Catholics now honor her as Saint Teresa of Calcutta.

how: The Missionaries of Charity run homes for the dying, the sick and abandoned children, and volunteers of any faith or none often help with washing, feeding and simply sitting with residents. Catholics keep her feast as Saint Teresa of Calcutta.

games.q: you teach in a convent school. outside the walls, people are dying in the street. what do you do?
o: keep teaching, and pray for the city.
ask permission to leave and live among the poorest.
raise money from inside the walls.
games.why: she asked to leave the convent and went out to live among the poor. the community she started became the Missionaries of Charity.

practice: Think of someone who is ill, or old, or alone a lot of the time: a neighbor, a grandparent, someone in a hospital bed, someone who eats by themselves.
See their face clearly and stay with them a while, the way a sister stays by a cot, without fixing anything. If you pray, hold them before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Mother Teresa. A nun who left her convent school to care for the dying and the abandoned, and who saw Jesus in each of them.

orig.note: Greek: "of the least" (Matthew 25:40), the people Jesus says he is found in.

carryVoice: Your line: do it for him. Unto one of the least of these. Nine hundred sixty-seven days, and counting.
